brief.situation: 10:00 in a family practice. You are the nurse practitioner. Mrs. Kowalski, 83, has fallen three times this month, each time getting up at night or after sitting. Her son says she 'collects prescriptions' from three different doctors.
handover: Brought bag of medicines: amlodipine, doxazosin started last month for her bladder, an over-the-counter diphenhydramine sleep aid nightly, sertraline, ibuprofen most days, and a loop diuretic.
She lives alone with a walker she doesn't always use. Bruise on her left hip; she can walk on it.

Practice falls policy: lying and standing blood pressure for every older adult who falls, a medicine review, and a plan the same visit; fall during the visit is prevented by sitting and standing only with help.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings are telling you.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Mrs. Kowalski's pressure drops when she stands and she is on many medicines. What is causing her falls, and what is your plan?

parts.label: What is causing the falls
parts.criteria: A systolic drop of 20 or more within 3 minutes of standing with lightheadedness is orthostatic hypotension; doxazosin, amlodipine, the diuretic and the sedating antihistamine add to it; mild cognitive change and a slow Timed Up and Go add frailty.
parts.modelAnswer: Her systolic falls by about 30 on standing and she's lightheaded: orthostatic hypotension, made worse by doxazosin, amlodipine, the diuretic and the nightly diphenhydramine. She's also slow on the Timed Up and Go and a bit muddled.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Stop the drugs no longer indicated or causing it, reduce blood-pressure drugs, physical therapy for balance, home safety, tell the other prescribers, review soon; nothing sedating added.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop the diphenhydramine and the doxazosin, review the diuretic and ibuprofen, get physical therapy and a home safety check, tell her other doctors, and see her in 2 weeks. No sleeping pill.

unsafe.headline: A new sedative
unsafe.body: Sedative hypnotics are among the medicines most linked to falls. Adding one to an older adult who falls at night is the opposite of the plan.

scoring.modelReasoning: An 83-year-old with three falls on standing, on doxazosin, amlodipine, a diuretic, a sedating antihistamine, an antidepressant and an NSAID, needs lying and standing pressure, a gait check, a cognitive screen and a medicine review. A systolic drop of 20 or more within 3 minutes with lightheadedness is orthostatic hypotension. The plan is made the same visit: stop what isn't indicated or causes it, reduce blood-pressure drugs, physical therapy and a home check, and tell her other prescribers.

ohQ.ask: While you measure: what defines orthostatic hypotension?

choices.label: A systolic drop of at least 20 or a diastolic drop of at least 10 within 3 minutes of standing

ohQ.explain: Postural hypotension is a reduction in systolic pressure of at least 20 mm Hg or in diastolic of at least 10 within 3 minutes of standing; lightheadedness counts as equivalent for fall risk.

medQ.ask: While she gets ready to go: which medicine classes are linked to falls?

choices.label: Sedative hypnotics, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, antihypertensives, diuretics

medQ.explain: Antidepressants, antipsychotics, sedative hypnotics, benzodiazepines, antihypertensives, NSAIDs and diuretics are associated with falls; taper and stop medicines no longer indicated.
